concepts.label: Clinical Workflow
concepts.summary: The actual sequence of tasks, decisions, and information exchanges that humans and systems perform to accomplish a clinical purpose. Distinct from process (broader), procedure (a single action), and protocol (the codified intended version).

concepts.label: Workflow Analysis
concepts.summary: The discipline of mapping what actually happens in clinical work — observing first, asking second, mapping the actual workflow rather than the intended one. Most informatics complaints have workflow underneath.

concepts.label: Swimlane Diagram
concepts.summary: Flowchart with horizontal lanes for actors and tasks placed in the lane of the actor performing them. Makes handoffs visible. Most common notation in clinical informatics analyses.

concepts.label: BPMN
concepts.summary: Business Process Model and Notation. Formal standard for process modeling with rich vocabulary (events, gateways, tasks, pools). Use when the analysis must be precise and shareable; overkill for most clinical conversations.

concepts.label: Value-Stream Mapping
concepts.summary: Lean / Toyota Production System notation that shows value flow with explicit annotations for time, waste, inventory, and waiting. Right notation when the question is 'where is the time going.'

concepts.label: Rework Loops
concepts.summary: Places where work is redone because of an upstream gap. One of three high-yield workflow failure patterns to look for. Often invisible to participants because they have learned to compensate.

concepts.label: Handoffs
concepts.summary: Transitions between actors in a workflow. Each handoff is an opportunity for information loss or distortion. Number of handoffs is one of the strongest predictors of error rate.

concepts.label: Workflow vs Process
concepts.summary: Process is the broader system-level sequence; workflow is the specific sequence to accomplish a clinical purpose. Procedure is a single action within the workflow. Protocol is the codified intended version.

concepts.label: Workarounds
concepts.summary: Deviations from the intended workflow that users invent to get work done despite system gaps, frictions, or mismatches. Should be treated as design feedback, not as discipline failures.

concepts.label: Usability (ISO 9241-11)
concepts.summary: The extent to which a system can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use. All three components matter.

concepts.label: Nielsen's Ten Heuristics
concepts.summary: Visibility of system status; match to real world; user control and freedom; consistency and standards; error prevention; recognition rather than recall; flexibility and efficiency of use; aesthetic and minimalist design; help users recover from errors; help and documentation.

concepts.label: Cognitive Load
concepts.summary: Three types: intrinsic (inherent task difficulty), extraneous (unnecessary mental effort imposed by system), germane (productive effort that contributes to learning). Reducing extraneous load is the highest-yield intervention for clinician burden.

concepts.label: Heuristic Evaluation
concepts.summary: Usability inspection method where 3–5 evaluators independently walk through a system against defined heuristics, then combine findings. Cheaper than usability testing; catches a substantial fraction of major problems.

concepts.label: Usability vs Satisfaction
concepts.summary: Satisfaction is one component of usability. A clinician who reports being satisfied may have adapted to poor usability rather than experiencing genuine usability. Objective task metrics matter alongside self-report.

concepts.label: User-Centered Design (UCD)
concepts.summary: The design philosophy that puts users at the center of every decision — observation, prototyping, testing, iteration, contextual inquiry. Opposite of design-and-ship-to-users-who-will-adapt.

concepts.label: Usability Testing
concepts.summary: Real users completing real tasks while the researcher observes and measures. More expensive and more diagnostic than heuristic evaluation. Tells you whether a fix actually worked.

concepts.label: Sociotechnical Model
concepts.summary: The framing that health IT is determined jointly by technology and by the humans, processes, organizations, and incentives wrapped around it. The unit of analysis is the system-in-context.

concepts.label: Sittig-Singh
concepts.summary: Dean Sittig and Hardeep Singh, authors of the eight-dimension sociotechnical model (2010, Quality and Safety in Health Care) and the SAFER Guides. The most-cited authors in clinical informatics safety.

concepts.label: Eight Sittig-Singh Dimensions
concepts.summary: (1) hardware/software; (2) clinical content; (3) human-computer interface; (4) people; (5) workflow and communication; (6) internal organizational policies/procedures/culture; (7) external rules/regulations/pressures; (8) system measurement and monitoring. Required board recall.

concepts.label: Dim 1 — Hardware and Software
concepts.summary: Servers, storage, network, OS, database, application code. Failures look like outages, slow response, capacity, bugs.

concepts.label: Dim 2 — Clinical Content
concepts.summary: Order sets, CDS rules, drug databases, problem lists, allergy dictionaries, templates, formulary, antibiograms. Where knowledge maintenance burden lives.

concepts.label: Dim 3 — Human-Computer Interface
concepts.summary: The screens and interactions through which users interact with the system. The usability dimension.

concepts.label: Dim 4 — People
concepts.summary: The humans who use, operate, support, and govern the system. Training, role mismatches, governance, key-person risk, vendor staffing.

concepts.label: Dim 5 — Workflow and Communication
concepts.summary: The sequence of tasks, handoffs, and information exchanges. The most consistently underweighted dimension and the one most often the actual cause of 'technical' failures.

concepts.label: Dim 6 — Internal Organizational Policies, Procedures, Culture
concepts.summary: Institution's rules, governance, decision-making, change management, risk tolerance, vendor relationship, history with prior projects.

concepts.label: Dim 7 — External Rules, Regulations, Pressures
concepts.summary: HIPAA, HITECH, Cures Act, ONC certification, Joint Commission, CMS measures, state laws, payer requirements.

concepts.label: Dim 8 — System Measurement and Monitoring
concepts.summary: Whether the institution actually looks at how the system is performing. Metrics, dashboards, audits, post-deployment evaluation. The dimension that distinguishes mature programs from immature ones.

concepts.label: SAFER Guides
concepts.summary: Nine voluntary self-assessment guides from ONC, developed by Sittig, Singh, and colleagues. First released 2014. Three categories (foundational, infrastructure, clinical process). Voluntary by design.

concepts.label: EHR Safety Self-Assessment
concepts.summary: The practice of running structured assessments (like SAFER) to identify gaps in EHR safety. Done internally rather than by external auditors.

concepts.label: High Priority Practices Guide
concepts.summary: The most important SAFER guide. Covers patient identification, communication of test results, electronic ordering, downtime planning, and organizational governance.

concepts.label: Organizational Responsibilities Guide
concepts.summary: SAFER guide on the leadership and governance structures for EHR safety. Who owns it. How decisions get made. How issues get escalated.

concepts.label: Patient Identification (SAFER)
concepts.summary: Practices ensuring each clinical action is associated with the correct patient: two-identifier verification, photo display, distinct visual treatment for active patient context, MPI hygiene.

concepts.label: CPOE with Decision Support (SAFER)
concepts.summary: SAFER guide on order entry and CDS practices: order set governance, alert tuning, override audits, content maintenance. Aligns with Module 4 content.

concepts.label: Test Results Reporting and Follow-up (SAFER)
concepts.summary: SAFER guide on the closed-loop reporting workflow, critical value notification, missed result tracking. The right channel for critical results is active notification, not passive secure messaging.

concepts.label: Downtime Planning
concepts.summary: Paper backup procedures, downtime training and drills, recovery protocols. The cyberattack scenario has become much more important since 2020 and SAFER guidance has been updated accordingly.
